author: janleike
text: Going forward, we want to train on harder tasks and decompose the evaluation of tasks instead of the tasks themselves. This way we can empower humans to evaluate our models and give value input even as tasks get very complex, while the model still learns to do the task end-to-end

author: janleike
text: The model interprets this as she getting asked for her hand in marriage. So when she says yes, it completely misrepresents the plot of the book.

author: janleike
text: An example from Pride & Prejudice I really liked: the protagonist gets asked “for their hand” at a dance, but the fact that it’s at a dance is not in the model’s context and got left out from summaries of previous pages.

author: janleike
text:
More importantly, we learned a bit about human supervision when decomposing tasks, e.g.:

* Compared to end-to-end training, it’s much easier to debug what the model is doing

* Sometimes there is important context missing when the model only does a small part of the overall task

author: janleike
text: We combine reward modeling and recursive task decomposition: the model summarizes a few pages at the time, then summarizes the summaries, and so on. The result is a model that actually writes plausible summaries of entire books, even matching average human quality 5% of the time.

author: janleike
text:
I'm very interested in techniques for supervising models to do tasks that are difficult for humans to evaluate.

To study this, we trained a model on summarizing entire books!

Read more 👇

https://t.co/sqfKCoymXO

author: janleike
text: Ideally the model should always write the best code, no matter how buggy the context. These kind of alignment problems are what we're trying to solve!

author: janleike
text: What is surprising is that the effect is quite strong: subtly buggy context degrades performance equivalent to a ~10x smaller model.

author: janleike
text: This is not surprising, given the nature of the training distribution: if a file contains bad code, it's more likely to contain more bad code, so guessing that bad code will follow is a good strategy for the model.

author: janleike
text: There are a lot of exciting things in the Codex paper, but my favorite titbit is the misalignment evaluations by @BethMayBarnes: Subtly buggy code in the context makes the model more likely to write buggy code, and this discrepancy gets larger as the models get bigger! https://t.co/nPiFngBW9t
